endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Verify adequacy of GAI system user instructions through user testing.

endorsements.title: Foundation for Artificial Intelligence-Driven Democratization of Healthcare Access
endorsements.quote: These design considerations must be complemented by the implementation of regular and methodologically rigorous usability audits of deployed systems, utilizing validated assessment instruments, to identify emergent barriers to effective utilization and opportunities for interface enhancement throughout the technology lifecycle [ 19 ].

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether measuring user satisfaction with the clarity of AI information improves clarity, use, or patient outcomes, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation currently rests on one federal framework and one commentary.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsements express expert opinion and do not supply comparative data on whether clarity measurement changes design decisions or user outcomes.

NIST AI 600-1 advises verifying the adequacy of generative AI user instructions through user testing. This is voluntary guidance rather than a binding FDA or ONC requirement. A second source, a commentary, calls for regular usability audits with validated instruments. Neither source specifies a satisfaction metric or a threshold for action.

No supplied study measured clarity satisfaction among patients or clinicians in any population. Satisfaction surveys that are offered only in English or at a high reading level may miss the users most likely to find AI output unclear. The current evidence cannot show whether this measurement reaches those groups.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without structured clarity feedback and that track whether the feedback leads to interface or content changes, higher comprehension, fewer errors, or lower rates of users abandoning the tool. Such studies should also test which validated instruments detect clarity problems in clinical settings.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether clarity measurement captures their experience, and any measurement they adopt would need translated, plain-language instruments to avoid excluding those users.
